newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Japanese, ADB loans to revive Sri Lanka plantation.
newsitem.headline: Japanese, ADB loans to revive Sri Lanka plantation.

text.p: Sri Lanka plans to revive its plantations industry, which is being privatised after years of neglect under state management, with the help of Japanese and Asian Development Bank (ADB) loans, industry officials said on Thursday.
"The aim is to increase productivity and to bring our plantations to a level competitive with other countries," a senior Plantations Industries Ministry official said.
"We want to enhance yield levels of tea, rubber and coconut estates and labour productivity."

Japan had extended $40 million and the ADB $60 million in soft loans to the Sri Lankan government to provide long-term development funds for capital development to privatised plantation companies, he said.

The bulk of the funds would be channelled through development and commercial banks while $20 million would be set aside for institutional development and forestry matters, along with social welfare such as workers quarters, training, health and sanitation facilities.
"Big, long-term investment loans are difficult to get from local banks," the ministry official said. "Interest rates are also high."

The firms have to submit five-year plans for field and factory development, and equipment, to get the loans on commercial terms just below the average weighted prime rate, officials said. There is a five-year grace period on repayment.
The Indian Ocean island is privatising its plantation firms which own some 600,000 hectares (1.48 million acres) of tea, rubber and coconut, once the mainstay of the country's economy.
Foreign companies are not allowed to control more than 49 percent of plantation companies.
In 1992, the government privatised management of 23 plantation firms.

It is now privatising ownership by selling 51 percent to a strategic investor, giving 10 percent to workers and selling the balance to the public on the Colombo Stock Exchange (CSE). The government retains one "golden share", which enables it to intervene in the case of mismanagement.
The once debt-ridden sector is recovering due to investments in replanting, fertiliser, machinery and value additions after privatisation.
"For the last so many years, capital investments in estates has been very low because the government had to incur considerable losses," a Tea Board official said.
"Also, under state ownership, companies would not invest in capital development," he added.
Private management firms project a 30 percent increase in tea yields in five years, he said.

"They have improved agricultural practices, increased profitability, cut losses -- there are visible changes in the field," he added. "These are long-term crops. It takes a few years to show results."
Sri Lanka needs to raise field productivity considerably to remain competitive after being plagued for years by low yields and poor labour productivity, analsyts said.
